sources.title: The Mordvinian People: History, Language and Culture
sources.note: Academic edited volume used only for broad historical, cultural, and writing-history framing; its unified terminology and retrospective reconstructions require caution.

sources.title: Revisiting the Etymology of the Ethnonym Mordva
sources.note: Peer-reviewed ethnonym study identifying Mordva as a Russian exoethnonym without roots in the Mordvinic languages and attested in medieval sources.

sources.title: The burial rite of Mordva on the Middle Tsna River, eighth to eleventh centuries
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology publication on mixed inhumation and cremation, varied graves and orientations, clothing traces, ornaments, tools, weapons, harness, paired burials, and interpretation.

sources.title: Historical phonology of the Mordvin languages
sources.note: Academic historical-linguistic reconstruction treating Erzya and Moksha as two languages and dating Proto-Mordvin divergence approximately rather than as a political event.

sources.title: Mordvin (Erzya and Moksha), Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages
sources.note: Peer-reviewed 2022 grammar: two languages, separate standards, dialects, corpus provenance, Cyrillic examples, glosses, and translations. Supplies the explicitly modern Moksha sample.

sources.title: The Erzya Language: Where is it spoken?
sources.note: Academic sociolinguistic profile: Mordvin is an exonymic umbrella; Erzya speakers identify their language by its own name; schooling and media evidence is modern.

sources.title: Names for the Mordvin idioms: historical and sociolinguistic approaches
sources.note: Academic synopsis stating that Mordvin is not a self-name and that Erzya and Moksha communities use their own names, with historical naming context.

sources.title: On linguistic distance between Erzya and Moksha
sources.note: University of Helsinki study measuring differences between the two related languages and warning against treating them as one uniform variety.

sources.title: Moksha Mordvin
sources.note: Peer-reviewed University of Helsinki chapter record for Moksha demographics, variation, grammar, authentic corpus examples, and an annotated text.

sources.title: Towards a systematic characterization of dialect variation in the Erzya-speaking world
sources.note: University of Helsinki research on Erzya dialect variation and differences from neighboring Moksha, supporting internal diversity.

sources.title: Mormula: Grammatically Annotated Mordvin Texts
sources.note: University of Turku corpus documenting separately identified Erzya and Moksha folklore, literary texts, dates, translations, and annotation.

sources.title: Diachronic Corpus of Literary Mordvin
sources.note: University of Turku corpus describing dated literary Erzya and Moksha sources and the much later record of written standards.

sources.title: MokshEr Corpus
sources.note: University of Turku corpus of modern journalistic and literary Erzya and Moksha, useful for modern continuity rather than medieval reconstruction.

sources.title: Culture and Language of Ancient Mordvinians
sources.note: University article on first- through seventh-century material and linguistic reconstructions; used as earlier comparison, not direct ninth-century proof.

sources.title: Shoksha cemetery publication
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology publication record for 900 graves at a fifth- to eleventh-century cemetery and competing cultural attributions by phase.

sources.title: Shoksha cemetery, volume 2
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology cemetery publication used for long chronology and continuing archaeological evidence across the atlas endpoint.

sources.title: Paired burials of the Middle Tsna Mordva
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology article on paired eighth- to eleventh-century burials, used narrowly for relationship possibilities and interpretive limits.

sources.title: Burial rite at the Kryukovo-Kuzhnovsky cemetery
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology article on Middle Tsna mortuary context and landscape, used separately from the broader 1993 synthesis.

sources.title: Early and medieval Mordvin ornament types
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology typological study of ornaments across long chronologies, supporting craft evidence without converting an object type into identity.

sources.title: Armiyevo cemetery study
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology study of 319 graves and eighth- to ninth-century interaction among local Finnic and Turkic-associated material networks.

sources.title: Finno-Ugric antiquities
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology publication statement warning that modern ethnicity differs from ancient archaeological categories and direct equations remain disputed.

sources.title: Belt sets in early medieval Volga-region burial contexts
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology study cautioning that belt fittings could be utilitarian, group-linked, or status-related and do not independently prove rank.

sources.title: Medieval Rus, Volga Bulgaria, and eastern contacts conference report
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology report noting that studied Bulgar belt sets entered ancient-Mordvin burial contexts in the tenth and eleventh centuries, after the atlas window.

sources.title: The Russian Primary Chronicle: Laurentian Text
sources.note: Harvard edition record for a twelfth-century compilation surviving in later manuscripts; its Mordva passage is later textual evidence, not an 800 CE census.

sources.title: The Russian Primary Chronicle, English translation
sources.note: University-hosted Cross and Sherbowitz-Wetzor translation listing Mordva among peoples with their own language; composed later than the atlas interval.

sources.title: Early Volga archaeological burial visibility and absence
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology discussion of uneven settlement and cemetery visibility and the danger of treating missing burials as an empty landscape.

sources.title: Four centuries of the chronicle Muroma
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology account of neighboring eighth- to eleventh-century Muroma cemeteries; used only as named comparative evidence, never as Mordvin identity.

sources.title: Mordva-Teryukhane: evidence of the past
sources.note: Lobachevsky University Museum synthesis of later medieval settlement finds, farming, fishing, beekeeping, crafts, pottery, textiles, and changing identity.

sources.title: Mordva-Teryukhane exhibition catalogue
sources.note: Lobachevsky University Museum catalogue for later medieval occupations, craft tools, furnishings, costume, and the collection context.

sources.title: Peoples of the Volga and Urals
sources.note: Russian Ethnographic Museum exhibit stressing a multiethnic region and materially documented later household crafts and rites.

sources.title: Mordovian Museum ethnography collection
sources.note: Official museum collection on the distinct peoples of Mordovia and cultural relations among Mordovian, Russian, and Tatar communities.

sources.title: Home and family in traditional Mordvin culture
sources.note: Peer-reviewed 2024 retrospective study of much later homes, family labor, inherited household marks, and changing domestic organization; not projected into 800 CE.

sources.title: Folk medicine of the Mordva: an ethnographic study
sources.note: Government humanities institute description of a 2011 study based mainly on 1991 to 2010 fieldwork, including plant, animal, mineral, surgical, and verbal practices.

sources.title: Research of traditional Mordovian medicine based on field trips
sources.note: Peer-reviewed ethnographic fieldwork article; its documented healing knowledge is modern evidence and cannot specify ninth-century remedies.

sources.title: The Mordovian family in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries
sources.note: Recent historical-ethnological study of family, modernization, identity, gender, language, and generational transmission in the modern period.

sources.title: Erzya bride costume, early twentieth century
sources.note: Russian Ethnographic Museum object record with exact date, place, materials, inherited use, and life-cycle context; explicitly modern comparison.

sources.title: Moksha headwear, nineteenth century
sources.note: Russian Ethnographic Museum object record with nineteenth-century date and materials; demonstrates distinct documented Moksha collection identity.

sources.title: Museum of Mordovian Culture and Everyday Life
sources.note: Official museum description of an early twentieth-century village interior, vessels, casks, clothing, farming tools, spinning, bast work, bathhouse, and granary.

sources.title: Mordva: historical and ethnographic essay
sources.note: Russian Geographical Society library record for a 1895 ethnographic work, useful as a dated historical source rather than timeless tradition.

sources.title: Mordva material in Estonian collections and Erzya and Moksha diasporas
sources.note: Peer-reviewed museum and diaspora study demonstrating later mobility, collecting histories, and continuing distinct Erzya and Moksha identities.

sources.title: Uralic Studies dissertation on Erzya and Moksha standards
sources.note: University dissertation describing the creation of separate standard Erzya and Moksha varieties in the twentieth century and their sociolinguistic setting.

sources.title: Russian Federal Archives: Mordovian autonomy anniversary
sources.note: Federal archival chronology distinguishing the 1928 Mordovian National Okrug from the older collective ethnonym.

sources.title: Erzyan songs, 1928 edition
sources.note: Russian National Electronic Library catalogue record for an Erzya publication dated 1928, tangible later written continuity rather than a medieval sample.

proposedOverrides.name: Erzya and Moksha communities (atlas: Mordvinians)
proposedOverrides.summary: An imported 800 to 900 culture layer whose modern external umbrella must not erase distinct Erzya and Moksha identities or become a fictional medieval state.
